wholeLesson.title: Ischemia, Electrolytes, and Medication Effects
wholeLesson.summary: Interpret ST, T, QRS and QT findings with symptoms, serial change, electrolyte measurements and medicine exposure. A nondiagnostic ECG cannot exclude dangerous hyperkalemia, and an apparent long QT requires measurement review.
wholeLesson.application: State the urgent clinical concern, compare prior and serial tracings, review potassium and magnesium with kidney function, and verify QT measurement and medicine exposure before choosing the response.

lesson.heading: Treat diagnostic acute ischemia as time sensitive
lesson.body: Interpret ST elevation across contiguous leads with symptoms, onset, morphology, reciprocal changes and the prior tracing. ST elevation alone does not prove acute coronary occlusion. When the clinical and ECG pattern is diagnostic, activate the emergency ischemia pathway without waiting for biomarker confirmation. A normal early troponin does not provide reassurance in that setting. Obtain additional posterior or right-sided leads when clinically indicated, and use serial ECGs when an initial tracing is nondiagnostic but suspicion persists.

lesson.heading: Keep the ST-T differential open
lesson.body: ST depression and T-wave inversion can reflect ischemia, reciprocal change, ventricular strain, bundle-branch block, pacing, electrolyte disturbance, medication effects or baseline variation. Review the involved leads, shape, change over time, QRS morphology and symptoms together. Neither one inverted T wave nor one nondiagnostic tracing establishes or excludes the clinical diagnosis.

lesson.heading: Assess potassium without waiting for a sequence
lesson.body: Hyperkalemia can produce peaked T waves, PR prolongation, reduced or absent P waves, QRS widening, bradycardia and dangerous arrhythmias. These findings need not appear in a fixed sequence, and severe hyperkalemia can have a nondiagnostic ECG. Assess measured potassium, sampling quality, kidney function, medicine exposures, symptoms and clinical acuity together. Promptly escalate clinically dangerous hyperkalemia rather than waiting for a sine wave or another textbook finding.

lesson.heading: Assess low potassium and magnesium together
lesson.body: Hypokalemia can flatten T waves, depress ST segments, produce prominent U waves and increase ventricular ectopy. Low magnesium contributes to repolarization instability and torsades risk, and can make potassium depletion difficult to correct. Review potassium and magnesium together with kidney function, diuretic exposure, gastrointestinal losses and other contributors. Correct the measured abnormalities and define rhythm monitoring according to the patient's risk rather than using ECG appearance alone to choose replacement.

lesson.heading: Verify where the T wave ends
lesson.body: QT extends from the beginning of the QRS to the end of the T wave. A prominent or fused U wave can make that endpoint difficult to identify; including it can produce an apparent long QT that actually includes the QU interval. Review the raw tracing in a lead with a clear T-wave end. Use a consistent measurement and correction method for comparisons, and reassess an automated value when rate, T-U morphology or QRS width makes it uncertain.

lesson.heading: Distinguish depolarization from repolarization effects
lesson.body: QT-active medicines can delay repolarization, while sodium-channel blockade can slow ventricular activation, widen QRS and alter the terminal axis. A widened QRS itself lengthens the measured QT; this alone does not establish acquired long-QT physiology or torsades risk. Review the exposure, waveform and clinical presentation together, and use an appropriate consistent method to assess repolarization when QRS is wide.

lesson.heading: Review the patient and the complete medicine list
lesson.body: Drug-associated torsades risk reflects dose and exposure, interacting and multiple QT-active medicines, potassium, magnesium, calcium, bradycardia, structural disease, age, sex and congenital susceptibility. Kidney and liver dysfunction can alter medicine exposure. Review symptoms, the baseline tracing and subsequent change, remove avoidable contributors, and select or discontinue treatment according to its benefit and risk. QT prolongation is a risk marker; it does not prove that torsades will occur.

keyPoints: Diagnostic acute ischemia should not wait for biomarker confirmation.
ST-T changes require a clinical differential.
Hyperkalemia need not follow a textbook ECG sequence.
A U wave or wide QRS can complicate QT interpretation.
Repolarization risk reflects both exposure and patient physiology.

check.question: Which statement about severe hyperkalemia is safest?
choices: A nondiagnostic ECG does not exclude it
It always produces a sine wave before danger
A normal QRS proves potassium is safe
Only QT prolongation occurs
check.rationale: Severe hyperkalemia may have no classic ECG changes. A normal QRS or the absence of a sine wave does not establish a safe potassium level. Use laboratory results, sampling quality and clinical acuity together, and respond promptly to dangerous hyperkalemia.

wholeQuestion.question: Which principle best characterizes hyperkalemia ECG evolution?
choices: Hyperkalemia can progress from peaked T waves and shortened repolarization to PR prolongation, P-wave loss, QRS widening, sine-wave pattern, and arrest, but ECG sensitivity is imperfect.
Every dangerous potassium level produces peaked T waves before conduction changes.
A normal QRS excludes severe hyperkalemia.
A sine-wave tracing is required before hyperkalemia can cause an arrhythmia.
wholeQuestion.rationale: The listed findings are possible manifestations, not a mandatory sequence or a reliable prediction of serum potassium. Severe hyperkalemia can have a nondiagnostic ECG, and dangerous arrhythmias can occur without preceding textbook changes.

wholeQuestion.question: Which reasoning hazard is most important to prevent with hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia?

wholeQuestion.rationale: Including a U wave can make a measured interval appear to be QT when it includes QU. The other choices are protective measurement and correlation steps. The tracing and a consistent method are needed rather than an automated number alone.

wholeQuestion.question: Which principle best characterizes QT-prolonging medications?
choices: Drug-associated torsades risk depends on QTc, dose and exposure, multiple QT drugs, electrolytes, bradycardia, structural disease, sex, age, and congenital susceptibility.
The presence of one QT-active medicine predicts torsades independently of the patient.

wholeQuestion.rationale: Drug-associated torsades risk combines exposure, interacting medicines, electrolytes, heart rate and patient vulnerability. Normality of one variable does not remove the others, and QT prolongation does not prove torsades will occur.

wholeQuestion.question: Which reasoning hazard is most important to prevent with QT-prolonging medications?
choices: Using one QTc cutoff without considering change, rate, QRS, and patient risk can misclassify danger.
Using a consistent measurement method when comparing baseline and follow-up tracings.
Reviewing QRS width and heart rate before interpreting an apparent long QT.
Considering electrolyte depletion and interacting exposure alongside the QTc.
wholeQuestion.rationale: One isolated cutoff can miss measurement problems and combined patient risk. The other choices address those problems. A widened QRS can lengthen QT through depolarization, so that alone does not establish acquired long-QT physiology.

finalComparisonNotes: Diagnostic clinical/ECG ischemia urgency is separate from isolated ST elevation; reject older obstruction shortcuts and assay timing.
Complete broad ST-T differential now has specific primary academic teaching evidence; reject source-caption absolute morphology rules.
Hyperkalemia manifestations and shortened repolarization are possible findings, not a required sequence or serum-potassium predictor; a nondiagnostic tracing cannot establish safety.
Low potassium/magnesium patterns require measured electrolytes and context; no replacement dose or universal monitoring schedule adopted.
QT/QU endpoint uncertainty and wide-QRS depolarization lengthening are separated from acquired long-QT physiology.
Dose, interactions, patient susceptibility, organ function and therapeutic benefit/risk remain combined rather than reducing judgment to one QT value.
